101|# PART I — The Chatbot Trap
102|
103|## Chapter 1 — The Great AI Disappointment
104|
105|![Chapter 1 — The Great AI Disappointment](images/ch01_ai_disappointment.png)
106|
107|I built a chatbot once. It was beautiful.
108|
109|I was running MIFECO, my logistics platform. We processed thousands of shipments per month, and our support team was drowning in the same questions: "Where's my shipment?" "When will it arrive?" "What's the status of order 48219?" So I built a customer-facing chatbot for our platform. I spent two weeks on the system prompt. I loaded it with every FAQ, every tracking API, every troubleshooting guide for stuck conveyor sensors. It was polite. It never hallucinated. It always apologized for the wait.
110|
111|It was a technical masterpiece. Our support ticket volume dropped exactly zero percent.
112|
113|Zero. Not a single support ticket saved. Customers kept calling and emailing exactly as they had before. The chatbot answered every question perfectly. It told people exactly where their shipment was. It explained billing in clear, step-by-step language. It walked customers through conveyor sensor troubleshooting with patience and precision. Nobody cared.
114|
115|"Why don't they use the chatbot?" I asked our support manager.
116|
117|"Because they don't want answers," she said. "They want their shipment un-stuck. They want the billing error fixed. They want the conveyor running again."
118|
119|That conversation changed everything I thought I knew about AI. I had built something that answered questions. My customers didn't need questions answered. They needed actions taken. Those are different things entirely.
120|
121|### What I Learned From a Perfect Chatbot That Did Nothing
122|
123|I spent the next eighteen months rebuilding. Not the chatbot — my entire approach. I stopped building things that wait for questions and started building things that do work. The result was our first production AI agent: a lead responder that captured inbound inquiries, checked order status, and sent updates automatically. No questions required. It just did the work.
124|
125|That first agent cost $2,812 and fourteen hours of my weekend to build. It replaced work that had been consuming twelve hours per week of a staff member's time. The payback period was two months. And it taught me something that no consultant, no book, and no conference keynote had ever said out loud: most business AI fails because it's designed to answer questions instead of taking action.
126|
127|This is the great AI disappointment of 2024 and 2025. Business owners heard the hype, bought the tools, built the assistants, and got nothing measurable out of them. I talk to founders and operators every week. The pattern is the same: they tried ChatGPT, they tried Claude, they tried the white-label chatbot platforms. Someone in the company spent serious time setting it up. And then nothing happened. No revenue increase. No headcount reduction. No process improvement. Just a chatbot sitting in a corner of the intranet answering questions that nobody was asking.
128|
129|The gap is between promise and reality. The promise was: AI will transform your business. The reality was: AI gives answers, and your business doesn't need more answers. Your business needs actions.
130|
131|Think about what actually runs a business. It's not the knowledge. it's the doing. Every deal that closes required someone to send a proposal. Every happy customer required someone to follow up. Every shipment that arrived on time required someone to check the schedule. Answers are passive. They sit there waiting to be consumed. Actions are active. They change the state of the world.
132|
133|A chatbot is a reference library with a friendly face. It's Wikipedia with small talk. It stores information and dispenses it on request. But your business doesn't suffer from a lack of stored information. Your business suffers from a lack of executed work.
134|
135|Any HVAC company doesn't need an onboarding bot. It needs onboarding to happen: background checks submitted, tool orders placed, truck assignments logged, first-day schedules sent, mentor assignments made. That's a dozen distinct actions per new hire. None of them involve asking a question. All of them involve doing something.
136|
137|This realization drove an architecture shift at one logistics company in particular. They started with a chatbot for their clients. They ended up building an agent system that takes actions in their platform and in their clients' systems. The difference wasn't the language model. It was the design: they stopped building things that wait for questions and started building things that do work.
138|
139|Here's the framework I've developed for thinking about this. Every business process has three layers: knowledge, decision, action. Knowledge is what you know. the policy, the procedure, the data. Decision is the logic that picks what to do given the knowledge. Action is the execution that changes something in the world. ChatGPT handles knowledge perfectly and decision adequately. It handles action not at all.
140|
141|If your business problem is knowledge. people don't know the 401k match percentage, people don't know the shipping cutoff time—a chatbot works. But most business problems aren't knowledge problems. They're action problems. The 401k match is known. What's missing is the enrollment form being submitted. The shipping cutoff time is known. What's missing is the order being placed before it.
142|
143|The lesson I took from that failed chatbot and from our own early failures is simple: if the AI can't do anything, it doesn't matter how much it knows. Your business runs on actions. Every system you buy, every person you hire, every process you build exists to cause something to happen. If the AI doesn't cause anything to happen, it's not a business tool. It's a parlor trick.
144|
145|This book is about the alternative. It's about agents. systems that take action. They don't wait for questions. They follow processes. They use tools. They make decisions within boundaries. They persist across time. And they do work, not just answer questions.
146|
147|By the end of this book, you'll know exactly what I mean by that, why it matters for your business, and how to start building it. But first we need to kill the chatbot illusion. You don't need a smarter FAQ. You need a worker that doesn't clock out.
148|
149|That chatbot is still running, by the way. It answers three questions a month, all from our support manager. Nobody else bothers. They just call support like they always did. The tool exists, the knowledge is there, but the behavior hasn't changed. Answers aren't the bottleneck. Action is.
150|
151|---
152|
153|**The One Thing**
154|
155|If your AI can't do anything, it doesn't matter how much it knows. Your business runs on actions — sending proposals, following up with leads, processing orders. If the AI doesn't cause anything to happen, it's not a business tool. It's a parlor trick. Build for action, not answers.
156|
157|
158|## Chapter 2 — Chatbot vs. Agent: Five Differences
159|
160|![Chapter 2 — Chatbot vs. Agent: Five Differences](images/ch02_chatbot_vs_agent.png)
161|
162|My wife asked me last month what I actually do all day. I said I build agents. She nodded and went back to her phone. A minute later she said, "So like Siri?" The gap between what most people think of as AI and what I'm actually building is wider than most business owners realize. And if you're going to invest in this, you need to see it clearly.
163|
164|A chatbot gives answers. An agent takes action. That's the simple version, but the details matter because the details determine what you can actually build. I've identified five practical differences between chatbots and agents that matter for business owners. These aren't academic distinctions. They directly determine whether the thing you build will produce revenue or sit in a forgotten browser tab.
165|
166|**First: Memory.**
167|
168|ChatGPT has what I call conversation memory. It remembers what you said two messages ago so it can maintain context within a single session. Close the tab, come back, and it's a blank slate. Your business processes don't work that way. A lead reaches out on Monday. Someone follows up on Wednesday. The deal closes two weeks later. Someone needs to remember the lead's company size, budget range, and the specific objection they raised on the first call.
169|
170|Agents maintain persistent memory. A lead outreach agent, for example, stores every interaction with every prospect in a structured database. It knows when a prospect asked for pricing but didn't open the follow-up quote. It knows which email templates have been sent, which calls have been scheduled, which objections have been raised. This isn't clever prompting. It's architecture. The agent writes to a database and reads from it before every action. It remembers because we built memory into the system, not because a language model happened to keep something in context.
171|
172|The business implication is huge. Without persistent memory, every interaction is a first date. You can't build relationships, you can't track progress, you can't learn from past failures. A chatbot that forgets everything between sessions isn't useful for anything beyond answering the same question twice.
173|
174|**Second: Autonomy.**
175|
176|Every chatbot waits for a question. That's the fundamental design. The user types, the chatbot answers. The user stops typing, the chatbot stops existing. It's purely reactive.
177|
178|Agents are proactive within their defined scope. Our pipeline outreach agent doesn't wait for someone to ask it to follow up. At 10 AM every day, it checks the schedule. If a prospect hasn't responded in three days, it sends a follow-up email. If a response comes in with certain keywords, it routes it to a human. If the prospect said "call me next week," it creates a calendar reminder and waits.
179|
180|This changes the economics of the system. A chatbot removes maybe a minute per question that someone would have spent searching. An agent removes entire workflows. Nobody has to remember to follow up. Nobody has to check whether the lead went cold. The agent just does it because that's how it was built.
181|
182|**Third: Tool Use.**
183|
184|ChatGPT can generate text. That's it. It can generate really good text, but it can't do anything else. It can't send an email, update a CRM record, schedule a meeting, run a report, or change a setting.
185|
186|An agent uses tools. An agent system typically has a set of capabilities: send email via an email API, create a contact in HubSpot, check calendar availability, generate a proposal PDF from a template, post a message to Slack. When the agent decides a prospect needs a proposal, it doesn't output a proposal draft for a human to copy-paste. It generates the PDF and sends it. The action completes.
187|
188|This is the single biggest difference in practical terms. A chatbot says "here's the answer." An agent says "I took care of it." One produces text. The other produces results.
189|
190|**Fourth: Persistence.**
191|
192|Chatbots exist only when someone is talking to them. They have no presence in your system outside of active conversations. They don't monitor. They don't watch. They don't trigger.
193|
194|Agents run continuously. Our lead qualification agent runs 24/7. It monitors our intake forms, our email inbox, and our calendar system. When a new lead submits a form, the agent is already processing it within seconds. It doesn't require someone to start a conversation. It's always there, watching its assigned territory.
195|
196|Think of it like a security guard versus an alarm system. A chatbot is a security guard who only works when you're standing in front of him asking questions. An agent is an alarm system that watches all the time and only alerts you when something happens.
197|
198|**Fifth: Decision-Making.**
199|
200|ChatGPT makes exactly one decision: what words to say next. It's a text prediction engine dressed up as intelligence. It's excellent at that, but it's also incredibly limited.
201|
202|Agents make operational decisions. Should I follow up now or wait? Should I route this to sales or support? Should I escalate to a human or handle it myself? These decisions require evaluation against rules, priorities, and business logic. The language model informs the decision, but the decision framework is separate.
203|
204|In one agent system I'm familiar with, the agent evaluates leads against a scoring model. If the lead is from a company with more than fifty employees and has visited the pricing page, the agent schedules a demo call. If the lead is from a company under ten employees and asked a general question, the agent sends an info packet. The language model generates the email text. The decision framework determines what happens. This separation is critical. You can change the rules without rewriting the prompts.
205|
206|The practical difference between all five of these capabilities is straightforward. A chatbot is a tool you use. An agent is a worker you manage. You use a hammer. You manage an employee. The relationship is different, the expectations are different, and the results are different.
207|
208|When you use a chatbot, you do the work of framing the question, interpreting the answer, and taking the action. The chatbot supports you while you do the work. When you manage an agent, you define the scope, set the boundaries, and review the results. The agent does the work.
209|
210|Most businesses that tried AI got a chatbot and expected an agent. They expected the AI to do work. Instead, they got a tool that produces text they still had to act on. No wonder they were disappointed.
211|
212|The five differences. memory, autonomy, tool use, persistence, decision-making—are the specification sheet for an agent system. If you're evaluating a vendor, building an internal tool, or just trying to understand what's possible, these are the five questions to ask. Does it remember between sessions? Does it act without being asked? Can it change things in the world? Does it run continuously? Does it make operational decisions or just generate text?
213|
214|If the answer to any of those is no, you're looking at a chatbot. And you already know what that gets you.
215|
216|
217|## Chapter 3 — Why Your CRM Can't Save You
218|
219|![Chapter 3 — Why Your CRM Can't Save You](images/ch03_crm_limits.png)
220|
221|Consider what happened at a mid-sized B2B company I'll call AlphaTech. In 2022, they spent forty-three thousand dollars on Salesforce. License fees, implementation consultant, custom fields, integrations with HubSpot and Mailchimp. Six months later, their sales pipeline looked exactly the same as it did before. Same number of leads. Same conversion rate. Same revenue. The only thing that changed was they had a really expensive database that nobody wanted to update.
222|
223|I'm not here to pick on Salesforce. Pick your poison. HubSpot, Pipedrive, Zoho, Freshsales. They're all the same thing: a database with a nice interface and some automation features bolted on. They're useful. I'm not saying you shouldn't have one. But if you think your CRM is going to solve your pipeline problems, you're wrong. Here's why.
224|
225|CRMs require data entry. That's their fundamental design constraint. The system doesn't know anything unless a human tells it. A lead calls, you take notes, you log the call. A prospect visits your pricing page, you log the visit. A deal progresses, you update the stage. Every piece of information in your CRM was put there by someone typing.
226|
227|This creates what I call the CRM maintenance tax. Every time someone enters data, they're not selling. Every minute spent updating fields, moving deals between stages, logging activities is a minute taken from actual revenue-generating work. Salespeople feel this. That's why CRM adoption rates hover around fifty percent in most organizations. The people who are supposed to use it don't want to, because using it takes time away from what they're measured on.
228|
229|The result is a database that's never quite accurate. Leads slip through because nobody logged the call. Deals sit in the wrong stage because nobody updated it. Follow-ups get missed because nobody set the reminder. The CRM becomes an aspirational record. what the sales team wishes was happening, not what's actually happening.
230|
231|Here's a real example from a company we'll call SwiftShip. They were using HubSpot to manage their logistics platform leads. A prospect would fill out the contact form, HubSpot would create a contact record, and then nothing. The contact would sit there until someone on their three-person sales team noticed it and did something. Sometimes that was ten minutes. Sometimes it was three days. Sometimes never. One lead came in on a Friday afternoon. The salesperson noticed it the following Wednesday. By then the prospect had already signed a contract with a competitor. I still have the email the prospect sent us when we finally called: "We reached out to you twice and never heard back. We went with someone else."
232|
233|SwiftShip analyzed six months of HubSpot data and found that thirty-seven percent of inbound leads never received any follow-up at all. Not a call. Not an email. Nothing. They filled out the form and went into the void. Those leads cost us money. we were paying for ads to generate them.
234|
235|The problem wasn't that we had the wrong CRM. The problem was that the CRM couldn't do anything. It could store a lead. It could show us a list of leads that needed attention. It could even send a notification. But it couldn't call the lead. It couldn't send a personalized email. It couldn't check whether we'd already sent a proposal. It couldn't follow up. It just sat there, a filing cabinet full of opportunities we were too busy to pursue.
236|
237|This is where agents change the equation. An agent doesn't need data entry because it performs data entry itself. It generates the information it needs through its own actions. Our lead agent doesn't wait for a salesperson to log a call. It makes the call, records the outcome, stores the notes, and updates the deal stage. The CRM becomes a byproduct of the agent's work, not the bottleneck.
238|
239|Think about the difference in information flow. In a CRM-dependent system, information flows like this: event happens, human notices, human opens CRM, human types information, information is stored. There are four handoffs, and three of them require human attention.
240|
241|In an agent-driven system, information flows like this: event happens, agent detects event, agent takes action, agent records action. One continuous process.
242|
243|The financial implications are direct. Every hour your sales team spends updating CRM fields is an hour they don't spend selling. If your average salesperson's fully loaded cost is one hundred thousand dollars a year, and they spend fifteen percent of their time on data entry, that's fifteen thousand dollars of lost selling capacity per person. For a team of ten, that's a hundred and fifty thousand dollars a year. That's not the cost of the CRM. That's the cost of the CRM's design limitation.
244|
245|But the bigger cost is the pipeline leaks that happen because the CRM can't act. Those thirty-seven percent of uncontacted leads at SwiftShip represented about sixty-two thousand dollars in potential revenue per month that they were systematically losing. Not because they didn't know they existed. They knew. HubSpot showed them to them. They just couldn't get to them.
246|
247|An agent doesn't have that problem. An agent can contact every lead. It doesn't get tired, it doesn't get busy, it doesn't prioritize the squeaky wheel. It processes the list. Every lead gets contacted. Every follow-up gets sent. Every deal stage gets updated.
248|
249|I'm not saying you should throw out your CRM. You should use one as a data store, not as an operations system. The CRM holds the records. The agent does the work. The CRM documents what happened. The agent makes things happen.
250|
251|If you're evaluating whether an agent system would help your business, look at your CRM first. Not at what it shows you. Look at what it's not showing you. the deals that should be there but aren't, the follow-ups that were supposed to happen but didn't, the leads that came in and disappeared. That gap between what your CRM says and what your pipeline actually needs is exactly where an agent earns its keep.
252|

301|When we finally called, they had already signed with a competitor. The prospect told us later, "We figured you weren't interested." We were interested. We were just disorganized.

313|This wasn't a sales team problem. We had good salespeople. They were busy. They focused on the leads that seemed most promising. They followed up with the people who followed up with them. 478|I've watched eight different businesses try to adopt AI agents. Three succeeded. Five failed. The failures all followed the same pattern. Week one: excitement. Week two: setup. Week three: demos. Week four: complications. Week five: frustration. Week six: abandonment.

480|The six-week death spiral is real. I've seen it play out multiple times. The first attempt at an agent system at one company I worked with died in exactly six weeks. They spent three weeks building something overly complex, two weeks trying to make it work, and one week admitting it wasn't working and quietly shutting it down. The pattern is so predictable that I can now spot it before it happens.
481|
482|Three things kill AI projects in the first six weeks. If you can avoid these three traps, you have a real shot at building something that lasts.
483|
484|**Trap one: scope creep.**
485|
486|The team starts with a clear goal. "We'll build a lead response agent." That's specific. That's manageable. But by the end of week two, someone has suggested adding features. "Can it also qualify leads?" Sure. "Can it update the CRM?" Easy. "Can it generate proposals?" That's more work, but fine. "Can it handle objections in live chat?" Now we're building a completely different system.
487|
488|This is how a two-week project becomes a six-week project that never finishes. Every feature addition multiplies the complexity. The lead response agent we started building needed to read email, generate text, and send it. Simple. The lead response plus qualification plus CRM update plus proposal generation plus live chat agent needed to integrate with three APIs, maintain state across multiple workflows, handle a dozen edge cases, and never make a mistake. That's a six-month engineering project, not a six-week pilot.
489|
490|The fix is brutal simplicity. Define exactly one thing the agent will do. Nothing else. Write it down. "This agent sends an initial response to every inbound lead within two minutes." That's the spec. Everything else is out of scope. If the agent does that one thing reliably, you've won. You can add features later. Schedule them for month two. Don't add them in week two. I've seen too many teams build a Swiss Army knife and end up with a tool that opens nothing well.
491|
492|**Trap two: tool addiction.**
493|
494|AI builders love tools. New models come out every week. New frameworks. New platforms. New vector databases. Each one promises to solve a problem you don't have yet. The team starts with a simple architecture. By week three, they're debating whether to switch from LangChain to CrewAI, whether to use GPT-4o or Claude 3.5, whether to store embeddings in Pinecone or Weaviate. None of these decisions matter for a simple agent. They're distractions.
495|
496|One team fell into this hard on their first attempt. They spent a week evaluating different language models, comparing latency benchmarks, reading blog posts about which framework was best. They never wrote a line of application code. They built a demo using three different frameworks and then couldn't figure out which one was causing the bugs.
497|
498|The fix is to pick the simplest possible stack and start building. Use the model you already have access to. Don't add a vector database until you have a use case that requires one. Don't switch frameworks because of a blog post. The first version of any agent should use the least number of technologies that could possibly work. You can optimize later.
499|
500|**Trap three: feedback loop abandonment.**
501|
502|This is the deadliest trap. The team builds the agent. They test it with sample inputs. It works. They deploy it to production. And then they stop looking at it.
503|
504|An agent in production is never finished. It encounters inputs you didn't anticipate. It makes mistakes you didn't plan for. It encounters edge cases that break your assumptions. If you don't watch it, review its outputs, and fix its failures, it will gradually degrade until it's producing garbage. And everyone will conclude the agent doesn't work.
505|
506|A first-gen agent at one organization worked beautifully for the first three days. Then a lead emailed in Spanish. The agent responded in English, never asked for clarification, and assigned a wrong priority score. Another lead asked a question the agent wasn't designed to answer. The agent hallucinated a response and promised a feature that didn't exist. Another lead had an email typo that bounced. The agent retried five times and then marked the lead as uninterested.
507|
508|The team wasn't watching. They were busy building the next feature. By the time they checked the logs, seven leads had received bad responses, one had complained to the support team, and a salesperson had to do damage control. They blamed the model. It wasn't the model's fault. It was their fault for not monitoring.
509|
510|The fix is a daily review ritual. Every morning, look at the agent's outputs from the previous day. Read the emails it sent. Check the decisions it made. Identify the mistakes. Fix them. Update the instructions. Add guardrails. The first month of any agent deployment requires daily attention. You're training the agent by correcting its mistakes, the same way you'd train a new employee. If you abandon the feedback loop, the agent stagnates.
511|
512|The businesses that succeed with agents treat deployment as the start of the process, not the end. They schedule monitoring time. They review logs. They iterate on prompts and rules based on actual production data. They accept that the first version will have flaws and they commit to fixing them.
513|
514|The businesses that fail treat deployment as the finish line. They build, launch, and move on to the next shiny thing. They expect perfection from a system that's never been tested against real-world conditions. They quit at the first sign of trouble, blaming the technology instead of their own process.
515|
516|The six-week death spiral is avoidable. Keep the scope to one thing. Use the simplest stack you can. Watch the outputs every day. If you do those three things, you'll still be running your agent six months from now. Most businesses won't. That's your advantage.

568|

571|When the time came to rebuild an AI stack the right way, the platform decision looked like it would take a weekend. It took three months, two false starts, and one very expensive lesson about vendor lock-in.
572|
573|Let me save you the trouble.
574|
575|There are three categories of AI agent platforms right now. The first is API providers like OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, and the model aggregators. You get raw access to language models, you pay per token, and you build everything else yourself. The second is custom platforms. LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, the framework layer. You get abstractions for chains, agents, tools, memory. You still need a hosting strategy. The third is no-code tools like Zapier AI, Relevance AI, and the new agent builders inside ChatGPT and Claude. You get drag-and-drop workflows, pre-built integrations, and a monthly subscription.
576|
577|Each category serves a different skill level and a different set of needs. The problem is that most people pick based on what's popular, not what fits.
578|
579|I'll give you my decision framework. It has three questions.
580|
581|Question one: can your team parse a JSON response? If the answer is no, you go no-code. Full stop. No-code platforms have limits. you can't customize tool behavior, you can't control the prompt temperature, you can't implement your own memory strategy. But if you can't build software, those limits don't matter because the alternative is nothing. Relevance AI and Zapier's agent builder are good starting points. They handle the basics: receive a message, process it, use a tool, return a result. You'll hit a wall eventually, but by then you'll know enough to decide whether to hire someone who can do the next level.
582|
583|Question two: do you need more than ten distinct tools? If yes, you need a custom platform. The no-code tools work fine for three to five integrations. Beyond that, the workflow graph becomes unmanageable. I watched a company try to build a customer support agent with fourteen tools in Zapier. The visual flow looked like plumbing in a chemical plant. They spent more time debugging tool routing than they would have writing code. Custom frameworks handle complexity through code, which scales linearly. Visual workflows scale exponentially in the wrong direction.
584|
585|Question three: is latency critical? If your agent needs to respond in under two seconds, you need direct API access, not an aggregator. Aggregators add routing overhead. OpenRouter typically adds 200 to 500 milliseconds per call. That's fine for email drafting or lead research. It's not fine for real-time customer service chat where a five-second pause breaks the conversation flow.

587|My choice was OpenRouter, and here is why.

589|A typical agent deployment runs multiple agents across different functions. The lead responder uses a fast, cheap model for initial triage. The contract reviewer uses a more capable, slower model. The logistics coordinator needs a model with good JSON mode for structured output.
590|
591|An aggregator like OpenRouter lets you route each agent to the optimal model without managing multiple API keys, billing accounts, and rate limits. One API key. One billing dashboard. One rate limit to monitor. If a model goes down, you switch to a fallback model in the configuration, not in the code.

593|You can also run a custom framework on top. Maybe you don't use LangChain or CrewAI. Maybe you build your own agent loop in your language of choice. About four hundred lines of core logic. How to format the response for the customer. The frameworks have defaults for all of these. Your defaults might be different.

595|The cost breakdown matters.
596|
597|An aggregator charges per token, usually ten to twenty percent less than direct API pricing because they buy in volume. A lead responder might cost about two cents per conversation. 598|
599|Using direct OpenAI API for the same volume might run around five hundred and fifty dollars. Using a no-code platform with per-seat pricing might cost more than two thousand dollars for the same throughput, without the ability to customize model selection.

615|## Chapter 12 — Anatomy of an Agent
616|
617|![Chapter 12 — Anatomy of an Agent](images/ch12_agent_anatomy.png)
618|
619|I spent a year building agents before I could explain what one actually is. Not the marketing version. the actual architecture. If you ask five AI vendors to define an agent, you get five different answers, and all of them make their product sound like the right one.
620|
621|Here is a working definition. An agent is a loop that takes in a prompt, decides what to do, uses tools to do it, remembers what happened, and learns from the outcome. Six components. Prompt, tool, decision, action, memory, learning. Each one has a concrete function. Each one can break independently.
622|
623|I will walk through each with real examples from our lead responder agent, because abstract explanations are useless.
624|
625|Component one is the prompt. Not the system prompt. the incoming prompt. This is the text the agent receives from a user, a system, or another agent. For the lead responder, the incoming prompt is a lead form submission. Name, company, email, phone, message. The raw text. The agent does not get a cleaned version. It gets exactly what the lead typed.
626|
627|This matters because real input is messy. People miss fields. They write "call me" instead of providing a phone number. They ask questions about pricing in the message field. The agent has to handle the mess, not the ideal version. I saw this happen when a first-generation agent assumed every submission had all fields filled. It didn't. The agent crashed on null values. They fixed that by sending the raw form data and letting the agent ask clarifying questions if something is missing.
628|
629|Component two is the tool. A tool is a function the agent can call. It has a name, a description, a set of parameters, and a return value. The agent does not execute the tool itself. It produces a structured call request, and the system executes it. This separation is critical. The agent suggests an action. The system enforces it.
630|
631|Our lead responder has five tools. CRM search looks up whether the contact already exists. Company enrichment pulls firmographic data from a business data API. Email drafting creates a personalized response template. Calendar check finds available slots. Lead scoring assigns a priority from one to five.
632|
633|Each tool has a description written for the agent, not for a human. For CRM search, the description says: "Use this to check if a contact or company already exists in the CRM. Returns record ID or null." For lead scoring, it says: "Rate this lead on a scale of 1 to 5 based on title, company size, and message intent. 5 means high priority."
634|
635|The quality of the tool description determines whether the agent calls the right tool at the right time. Bad descriptions cause the agent to misuse tools. Good descriptions make the agent's decisions obvious.
636|
637|Component three is the decision. This is the reasoning step. The agent looks at the incoming prompt and the available tools and decides what to do. In practice, this is a language model call with a structured output format. The agent produces a JSON object: which tool to call, with what parameters, and what the expected outcome is.
638|
639|The decision step is where most failures happen. The agent picks the wrong tool. It uses CRM search when it should use company enrichment. It calls lead scoring before checking if the lead is a duplicate. These are logical errors, not language errors. They happen because the agent does not have enough context about the business process.
640|
641|One fix is to add a step dependency map to the system prompt. The map says: always check CRM first, then enrich, then score, then draft. The agent can deviate if the situation calls for it, but the default path is defined. Decision accuracy went from seventy-two percent to ninety-four percent in one week.
642|
643|Component four is the action. This is the execution. The system takes the agent's tool call request, validates it against the tool schema, executes the function, and returns the result. The agent does not execute anything. It only decides. The action layer enforces permissions, rate limits, and data access.
644|
645|This separation saves systems from disaster. For example, an agent might decide it should delete duplicate CRM records. It generates a delete tool call. But the action layer doesn't have a delete tool. Only the CRM team has delete access. The agent can suggest deletions, but it cannot execute them. The action layer is your safety net. Design it to be suspicious of every tool call.
646|
647|Component five is memory. The agent needs to remember what it already did. This is not about long-term knowledge. It is about the current session. The lead responder checks CRM, then enriches, then scores, then drafts. Each step depends on the previous step's result. The memory keeps the conversation state: what tools were called, what data was returned, what the agent already decided.
648|
649|Without memory, the agent calls the same tool twice, or it drafts an email without the enrichment data. Our first implementation had no memory beyond the raw message history. The agent would check CRM, get a result, and then check CRM again because it forgot. Adding explicit session state cut tool calls by forty percent and reduced latency by half.
650|
651|Component six is learning. This is the least developed component in most agents, including ours. Learning means the agent improves over time based on outcomes. Did the lead respond to the email? Did the contract get signed? Did the support ticket close?
652|
653|I have a simple feedback loop. For every completed agent run, we log the outcome as success or failure. Failed runs are reviewed weekly. We adjust prompts, add tools, or modify decision rules based on the pattern of failures. This is not automatic learning. It is human-in-the-loop learning. But it works.
654|
655|Automatic learning. where the agent modifies its own prompts or decision logic based on outcomes—is a research problem, not a production solution. I have seen companies claim they do this. I have not seen it work reliably outside of controlled lab conditions.
656|
657|The lead responder after six months of this loop is noticeably better than the one we started with. It asks fewer redundant questions. It catches leads it used to miss. It sends better drafts. The improvement came from analyzing failures every Friday afternoon. Not from a smarter model.
658|
659|An agent is not a chatbot with tools. A chatbot with tools is a chatbot that can look things up. An agent is a system that receives input, reasons about it, takes action, remembers the context, and improves over time. The difference is not in the language model. It is in the loop.

661|## Chapter 13 — Your First Agent
662|
663|![Chapter 13 — Your First Agent](images/ch13_first_agent.png)
664|
665|The first agent you build should not be the most important one. It should be the most forgiving one. Something that matters enough to measure but not so much that failure costs you a customer.
666|
667|A lead responder is the classic example. It handles incoming sales inquiries. If it makes a mistake, a human reviews and fixes it before the lead ever sees the mistake. Low risk, high visibility. Perfect for a first build.
668|
669|I am going to walk you through the exact build. Not the theory. The steps. The prompts. The gotchas. You should be able to replicate this in a weekend.
670|
671|Step one is defining the workflow. Before you write any code or configure any no-code tool, write down the steps a human takes when a lead comes in. The best way to start is to sit with your sales development rep for an hour. Watch them handle twenty leads. Here is what they do.
672|
673|Check if the lead already exists in CRM. If yes, check the last contact date. If contacted within thirty days, mark as duplicate and skip. If not, look up the company. How many employees. What industry. What tech stack. Then read the lead message. What are they asking about. What is their intent. Then score the lead. High, medium, low. High gets a same-day call attempt. Medium gets a personalized email within four hours. Low gets added to the nurture sequence. Then draft the outreach. High leads get a short, direct email mentioning the specific product or feature they asked about. Medium leads get a longer educational email. Low leads get a generic introduction. Then log everything in CRM and send the draft to the rep for review.
674|
675|That is the workflow. Six steps. Five tool calls. One human review.
676|
677|Step two is writing the system prompt. I am going to give you the template we use. Do not copy it exactly. Adapt it to your business. But the structure is important.
678|
679|The prompt has three sections. Role, rules, examples.
680|
681|Role tells the agent who it is. Not a vague personality. A specific job function. Here's an example: "You are a lead qualification and outreach assistant. You work for the sales team. Your job is to process incoming leads, research them, score them, and draft initial outreach. You do not send anything without human approval."
682|
683|Rules are non-negotiable constraints. We have five. Do not make up information about a lead or company. If a tool call fails or returns empty, report the failure and ask for manual intervention. Always check for duplicates before doing any research. Never disclose pricing in the first message. Never send an email without a human reviewing it first.
684|
685|Examples show the agent what good output looks like. We include three examples of completed lead processing. One high-score lead with a full company profile. One medium-score lead with partial information. One duplicate lead that got flagged and skipped.
686|
687|The examples are the most important part. Without them, the agent invents its own format and the output is inconsistent. With them, ninety-five percent of outputs follow the exact structure we want.
688|
689|Step three is building the tools. Start with two. Do not build five. Start with two and add as you see the agent struggle.
690|
691|Our first two tools were CRM search and email draft. That was enough to process simple leads. We added company enrichment in week two after the agent kept sending emails to leads at companies we could not evaluate. We added lead scoring in week three after the agent treated every lead the same. We added calendar check in month two after the sales team asked for it.
692|
693|The tool descriptions matter more than the tool implementation. Spend more time on the description than on the code. A well-typed function with a bad description is useless. A mediocre function with a great description works fine.
694|
695|Step four is building the review queue. This is the safety net. Every lead processed by the agent goes into a queue. Jen opens it every morning. She sees the agent's work: duplicate check result, company profile, lead score, and draft email. She can approve, edit, or reject each one.
696|
697|The review queue is a simple web page. Three columns. Pending, approved, rejected. Each card shows the original lead, the agent's output, and action buttons. Took our developer two days to build. Index page, detail page, approve button, reject button. That is it.
698|
699|The approval rate typically starts at around sixty percent. After two weeks of tweaking, it hits eighty-five percent. After the prompt examples are refined, it can hit ninety-three percent. The remaining seven percent are edge cases the agent cannot handle. leads in languages you don't support, requests for partnerships instead of purchases, people asking for jobs instead of products. Those get manually handled.
700|
701|Step five is the handoff. When a lead is approved, the agent sends the email and logs the activity in CRM. The agent does not send directly. It generates the send request, the action layer validates it, and the action layer places the call to the email API. The agent never touches the send button.
702|
703|This separation means that even if the agent hallucinates and produces a bad email, no email goes out until a human says yes. The agent cannot spam a lead. It cannot email the wrong person. It can only suggest.
704|
705|The total build time for a lead responder might be four days. Day one for workflow definition and prompt writing. Day two for tool building. Day three for the review queue. Day four for integration and testing.
706|
707|The ongoing maintenance is thirty minutes per week. The human reviews the failed leads, you update the prompt examples based on what they find, and you move on.
708|
709|Here is a concrete measurement. Before the agent, a rep processed about fifteen leads per day. That was their ceiling. After the agent, they process about forty per day. The agent does the research, scoring, and drafting. The human does the reviewing and the actual selling. Their close rate goes up because they spend more time talking to leads and less time typing.
710|
711|That is the pattern. Your first agent should not replace a person. It should make a person more effective.

713|## Chapter 14 — Giving Your Agent Tools
714|
715|![Chapter 14 — Giving Your Agent Tools](images/ch14_agent_tools.png)
716|
717|An agent without tools is a parrot. It can repeat information. It cannot change anything. The power of an agent comes from what it can reach: your email system, your calendar, your CRM, your database, your shipping platform, your payment processor.
718|
719|But connecting an agent to your tools is where most implementations break. The agent gets too much access and causes damage. Or it gets too little and cannot do anything useful. Finding the balance is the hardest engineering decision you will make.
720|
721|Here are three integration methods worth understanding, the permission model that keeps us out of trouble, and the distinction between talking and acting that every agent builder needs to understand.
722|
723|Method one is webhooks. This is the simplest integration. Your agent constructs an HTTP request to a webhook URL, and the receiving system processes it. Webhooks work for sending data outward. They do not work for fetching data. If your agent needs to look something up, webhooks are not the answer.
724|
725|We use webhooks for actions that are fire-and-forget. When the lead responder processes a lead, it fires a webhook to our Slack channel with the lead summary. The webhook takes a JSON payload, Slack renders it, done. No response expected. No error handling needed beyond a retry.
726|
727|Method two is APIs. This is the standard approach. Your agent calls an authenticated REST endpoint, sends parameters, gets a response. APIs work for both reading and writing. They also introduce complexity: authentication, rate limits, error handling, pagination.
728|
729|A logistics coordinator agent might call the shipping API about two hundred times per day. It checks shipment status, updates delivery windows, and flags exceptions. Each call requires an API key with specific scope. The agent cannot cancel shipments because the API key does not have cancel permission. The system enforces this at the API level, not the agent level.
730|
731|Method three is MCP, the Model Context Protocol. This is the newest approach and the one I am most excited about. MCP is a standardized protocol for connecting language models to tools. Instead of writing a custom integration for every tool, you write an MCP server that exposes your tool functions, and any MCP-compatible agent can use them.
732|
733|The protocol handles the handshake, the tool discovery, and the call-and-response format. You define your tools once in a standard schema. Any agent that speaks MCP can discover and call them. This is the opposite of the current norm, where every agent framework has its own tool format and you write adapters between them.
734|
735|Imagine switching a CRM integration to MCP. One MCP server, about three hundred lines of TypeScript, exposes five tools: contact lookup, contact create, deal lookup, deal update, activity log. Any agent in the system can now call any of these tools without a custom integration. The lead responder uses three of them. The contract reviewer uses two. The reporting agent uses one. Same server, different agents, no duplicated code.
736|
737|The practical benefit is maintenance. Before MCP, every agent had its own CRM integration code. If the CRM API changes, you have to update four separate code paths. With MCP, you update one server and all agents pick up the change immediately.
738|
739|The permission model is where most people get this wrong. They give the agent broad access and rely on the agent's judgment to use it correctly. That is a mistake. Agent judgment is unreliable. You need hard enforcement at the tool level.
740|
741|I use three permission tiers.
742|
743|Tier one is read-only. The agent can look up data but cannot change it. CRM search, calendar view, document retrieval. This is the default for any new tool. The agent does not get write access until we observe it handling read access correctly for at least two weeks.
744|
745|Tier two is write-with-approval. The agent can suggest changes, but a human must approve them before execution. Email draft, contract update, deal stage change. The agent writes the content. A human reviews it. The system only executes after the approval signal.
746|
747|Tier three is write-auto. The agent can make changes autonomously. Only applies to low-risk, high-frequency actions. Logging activity records. Updating lead scores. Sending automated follow-up emails after a deal closes. We audit tier three actions daily.
748|
749|Here is a concrete example of the permission model in action.
750|
751|A logistics coordinator can check shipment status from any carrier. Read-only. It can suggest delivery window updates when a shipment is delayed. Write-with-approval. It can log tracking events to the database. Write-auto. An escalation handler can create support tickets. Write-auto. It should not be able to cancel orders — it simply doesn't have that capability.
752|
753|The cancellation example is worth dwelling on. Consider an early version of a system with a tool that could cancel orders. The description said "Cancel an order by ID." During testing, the agent interpreted a customer complaint about a late shipment as a request to cancel all of that customer's orders. It generated six cancel calls before the action layer blocked it because of a rate limit. The cancel tool was removed entirely. If cancellation is needed, a human does it.
754|
755|The distinction between talking and acting is the framework that guides all of this.
756|
757|Talking means the agent says something. It drafts an email, generates a summary, answers a question. Talking is low risk. The worst outcome is that the agent says something slightly wrong and a human corrects it.
758|
759|Acting means the agent changes something. It submits a form, updates a database record, sends a message, creates an invoice. Acting is high risk. The worst outcome is that the agent does something irreversible.
760|
761|My rule: default to talking, escalate to acting only when the cost of inaction exceeds the cost of a mistake.
762|
763|The lead responder talks. it drafts emails. It does not act—it does not send them. The logistics coordinator talks—it suggests delivery window changes. It acts on one thing—logging tracking events, which is low-risk and high-frequency.
764|
765|Your agents should follow the same pattern. Give them plenty of talking tools. Give them acting tools sparingly, with approval gates, and with hard permission enforcement at the integration layer, not the agent layer. The agent can suggest anything it wants. The tool system only executes what is allowed.
766|
767|## Chapter 15 — Human-in-the-Loop
768|
769|![Chapter 15 — Human-in-the-Loop](images/ch15_human_in_loop.png)
770|
771|The question I get most often from other founders is not about technology. It is about trust. "How do I know the agent will not screw something up?" The answer is that you do not know. So you design for that uncertainty.
772|
773|I use three modes for agent operation. Full auto, where the agent acts without approval. Approve-first, where the agent proposes and a human authorizes. Review-after, where the agent acts immediately and a human inspects the result later. Each mode serves a different function. Picking the wrong mode for a given function is where the real failures happen.
774|
775|Full auto is for actions where speed matters more than perfection, and the cost of a mistake is low. A monitoring agent typically runs in full auto. It checks system health metrics every five minutes. If it detects an anomaly. CPU spike, error rate jump, queue backlog—it creates a diagnostic report and posts it to our incident channel. It does not ask permission. It just does it. The cost of a false alarm is a few seconds of reading time. The cost of a missed alarm is a production outage. Full auto is the right call.
776|
777|Another full auto example is our logging agent. Every agent run is logged with a structured record: prompt, tool calls, decisions, outcome. The logging agent writes these to the database automatically. If it wrote a bad record, I would notice in the weekly review. If it failed to write a record, I would have no audit trail. Full auto ensures the audit trail exists.
778|
779|Approve-first is for actions where accuracy matters and a human can add value by reviewing before execution. This is where most of our agents operate. The lead responder drafts emails but does not send them until Jenny approves. The contract reviewer flags unusual clauses but does not suggest redlines until legal reviews. The escalation handler proposes a resolution path but does not execute it until the shift lead confirms.
780|
781|Approve-first adds latency. The lead responder's email sits in a queue for an average of forty minutes before someone reviews it. That is forty minutes slower than a fully automated system. But it is also forty minutes of protection against the kind of mistake that costs a customer relationship.
782|
783|Here's a real cautionary tale. A lead responder was run in full auto mode for a week. It sent one hundred and thirty-seven emails. One of them contained a pricing hallucination. The agent quoted a price thirty percent below the actual rate. The lead replied and wanted to buy at that price. The company had to honor it because the email came from their domain. That mistake cost about twelve hundred dollars in margin. Approve-first would have caught it because a human would have seen the price and corrected it before send.
784|
785|Review-after is for actions where execution speed is critical and the review can happen asynchronously. A logistics coordinator typically runs in review-after mode. When a shipment is delayed, the agent updates the delivery window in the customer portal immediately. Then it flags the update for review. The logistics team checks the flagged updates at the end of each shift. By then, most customers have already seen the updated window and adjusted their plans. If the update was wrong, the team corrects it and the customer gets a notification. The cost of a wrong update is a correction. The benefit of an immediate update is customer trust.
786|
787|The framework I use to decide which mode to use has three variables.
788|
789|First variable: reversibility. Can the action be undone? Sending an email is irreversible. Updating a lead score is reversible. Creating a support ticket is reversible. Deleting a record is not. Irreversible actions default to approve-first. Reversible actions can go up to review-after or full auto depending on the other variables.
790|
791|Second variable: velocity. How fast does the action need to happen? A shipment delay notification needs to happen within minutes. A contract review can take hours. A lead response can take tens of minutes. Higher velocity pushes toward full auto or review-after. Lower velocity pushes toward approve-first.
792|
793|Third variable: confidence. How sure are we that the agent will make the right call? Confidence comes from testing. If the agent has processed a thousand similar cases with a ninety-five percent accuracy rate, confidence is high. If the agent is new or the use case is novel, confidence is low. Low confidence means approve-first. High confidence means consider full auto or review-after.
794|
795|The three variables form a decision matrix. High irreversibility plus low confidence equals approve-first. Low irreversibility plus high velocity plus moderate confidence equals review-after. Low irreversibility plus high confidence equals full auto.
796|
797|Here is how this plays out for a function we added recently. The reporting agent sends weekly performance summaries to department heads. The action is sending an email with a PDF attachment. Irreversibility is low. the email can be recalled or followed up with a correction. Velocity is low—weekly reports are not urgent. Confidence is high after three months of testing. So we run it in full auto. The agent generates the report, attaches the PDF, and sends it. No review. No approval. It has been running for six weeks without a mistake.
798|
799|Compare that to the customer-facing price quote agent. Same action. sending an email with a document. But irreversibility is high—a wrong price quote is legally binding in many cases. Velocity is moderate—customers expect a quote within hours, not days. Confidence is moderate after testing. So we run it in review-after, but with a twist. The agent sends the quote to the customer and CCs the sales rep. The rep sees the quote immediately and can follow up if anything is wrong. The quote goes out fast, but the rep has eyes on it within seconds.
800|
801|The mistake most companies make is choosing one mode for everything. They either lock everything down with approve-first, killing speed, or they let everything run on full auto, creating risk. The right approach is per-function mode selection, reviewed and adjusted monthly.
802|
803|The recommended approach is a spreadsheet. One row per agent. Columns for function, mode, justification, and incident count. If an agent has zero incidents in its current mode for three months, I consider moving it to a less restrictive mode. If an agent has incidents, I move it to a more restrictive mode.
804|
805|The goal is not to eliminate human involvement. The goal is to put human involvement exactly where it adds value and remove it where it adds delay.
806|
807|## Chapter 16 — Memory: Why Agents Forget
808|
809|![Chapter 16 — Memory: Why Agents Forget](images/ch16_agent_memory.png)
810|
811|Consider a conversation with a logistics coordinator agent that might make you want to throw your laptop out the window.
812|
813|"Check shipment 44982," I said.
814|
815|The agent checked. "Shipment 44982 is delayed. The new estimated delivery is Tuesday."
816|
817|"What was the original delivery date?"
818|
819|The agent paused. Then it called the shipment API again, looking for the original date. It found it. "Monday."
820|
821|"Check shipment 44983," I said.
822|
823|The agent checked. "Shipment 44983 is on time."
824|
825|"And what about the delayed one? 44982?"
826|
827|The agent did not know what I was talking about. It had already forgotten about 44982. It asked me to clarify which shipment I meant. I had just told it. Twenty seconds earlier.
828|
829|This is the fundamental problem with agent memory. The agents do not remember anything beyond their immediate context window unless you explicitly build memory into the system. The language model has no persistent state. Every interaction starts fresh.
830|
831|There are two kinds of memory you need to understand. Short-term memory is the conversation window. The current session. What the agent just did. Long-term memory is persistent storage. Information the agent can access across sessions.
832|
833|Short-term memory is handled by the context window. Every time the agent makes a decision, generates a response, or calls a tool, the history of that interaction gets appended to the next request. The model sees everything that happened so far in this session.
834|
835|The limit is the context window size. Most models support between 8,000 and 128,000 tokens. A token is roughly three-quarters of a word. So 128,000 tokens is about 96,000 words. That sounds like a lot. It is not.
836|
837|Every tool call eats tokens. The tool description. The parameters. The return value. A single CRM lookup can consume 500 tokens. A company enrichment call consumes 1,000. An email draft consumes 1,500. After ten interactions, you have used 30,000 tokens just on tool overhead. The actual conversation is a fraction of that.
838|
839|One approach to the short-term memory problem is a sliding window. We keep the last three interactions plus a summary of everything before that. The summary is generated by the agent itself. After every fifth interaction, the agent produces a one-paragraph summary of the conversation so far. That summary replaces the older history in the next context window.
840|
841|This approach keeps our costs predictable. Each agent run costs between 2,000 and 5,000 tokens, depending on complexity. Without the sliding window, a long-running agent session could hit 50,000 tokens. At that point, the cost of the conversation exceeds the value of the work being done.
842|
843|Long-term memory is a different problem. The agent needs to remember facts across sessions. Customer preferences. Previous orders. Past interactions. This is not something the language model handles naturally. You have to build it.
844|
845|Several approaches can be tried before finding one that works. The first was storing everything in a vector database. Every interaction was embedded and stored. When a new interaction started, the agent searched for relevant past interactions and injected them into the context. This is the standard RAG approach. It worked poorly for us. The agent pulled up irrelevant memories, missed relevant ones, and spent more tokens reading old conversations than handling new ones.
846|
847|The second approach was structured memory. Instead of storing raw conversations, we store structured facts. Customer X prefers email over phone. Customer Y has a net-60 payment term. Customer Z always complains about shipping speed. These are key-value pairs stored in a simple database. The agent queries them by customer ID when a session starts.
848|
849|This works better. The agent gets exactly the information it needs, no more. The token cost is minimal because the facts are short and targeted. The downside is maintenance. Someone has to write the facts. Our agents can suggest facts to add to memory, but a human reviews and approves them before they go in.
850|
851|The third approach, which is what we use now, is a hybrid. Short-term memory uses the sliding window with summaries. Long-term memory uses structured facts with human approval. But we also have a third layer: operational memory.
852|
853|Operational memory is the state of the agent's work. What tasks are in progress. What tools have been called. What decisions have been made. This is stored in a JSON object that persists for the duration of a workflow. When the lead responder processes a lead, the operational memory tracks the current step. Step one: CRM check complete. Step two: enrichment in progress. Step three: scoring pending. If the agent gets interrupted, it picks up from the last completed step.
854|
855|This matters more than you might think. Agents fail. API calls time out. Model responses are malformed. The user closes the browser. Operational memory means the agent does not start over. It resumes.
856|
857|The cost trade-off is straightforward.
858|
859|More memory means more tokens per call. Tokens cost money. At our volume, each additional 1,000 tokens of memory costs about three cents. Over twenty thousand runs per month, that is six hundred dollars for a modest increase in memory depth.
860|
861|Less memory means the agent forgets things and makes mistakes. Each mistake costs time. Jenny spends twenty minutes fixing an agent error. At her hourly rate, that is about ten dollars per mistake. If the agent makes five mistakes per week due to memory failures, that is two hundred dollars per week.
862|
863|The math says invest in memory until the token cost exceeds the mistake cost. For us, that point is around four thousand tokens of context per agent run. That includes the sliding window history, the structured facts, and the operational memory.
864|
865|Here is what I recommend for someone starting out. Do not build a vector database on day one. Start with no memory beyond the raw conversation window. See where the agent fails. Add a summary window when conversations exceed ten turns. Add structured facts when the agent starts repeating itself across sessions. Add operational memory when the agent cannot handle interruptions.
866|
867|Each layer solves a specific failure mode. Adding all three at once is overengineering. Adding none of them means your agent will forget what it did twenty seconds ago, and you will want to throw your laptop out the window.
868|
869|## Chapter 17 — Prompt Design (Not Engineering)
870|
871|![Chapter 17 — Prompt Design (Not Engineering)](images/ch17_prompt_design.png)
872|
873|I hate the term prompt engineering. It implies that writing good prompts is a technical skill on par with writing good code. It is not. Prompting is writing. It is clear communication with an AI system. You do not need to be an engineer to be good at it. You need to be precise.
874|
875|The difference between a prompt that works once and a prompt that works reliably is structure. A one-shot prompt is something you write for a specific situation. You are asking the model a question, you get an answer, you move on. A reliable prompt is something you write for production. It runs hundreds or thousands of times. It handles edge cases. It produces consistent output.
876|
877|Every production prompt typically follows the same template. Role, rules, examples. Three sections. No deviations.
878|
879|The role section defines who the agent is and what it is supposed to do. I wrote earlier about the lead responder's role. Let me show you the exact text.
880|
881|"You are a lead qualification and outreach assistant for MIFECO, a logistics technology company. You work for the sales team. Your job is to process incoming leads from the website contact form. You research the lead and their company, score the lead on a scale of 1 to 5, and draft a personalized initial email. You do not send the email. You submit it for human review. You never make up information about a lead or company. If you cannot find reliable information, you note the gap and proceed with what you have."
882|
883|That is the role section. It establishes identity, function, boundaries, and failure mode. It tells the agent what to do, what not to do, and what to do when things go wrong.
884|
885|The role section is not a personality. It is a job description. I do not tell the agent to be friendly, helpful, or professional. Those are vague, and the agent interprets them differently every time. I tell the agent exactly what steps to follow and exactly what constraints to respect.
886|
887|The rules section lists constraints. Every rule is a specific behavior, not a general principle.
888|
889|Rule one: always check CRM for existing records before doing any research. Rule two: if the CRM check returns a record with contact date within thirty days, mark as duplicate and skip. Rule three: use the company enrichment tool before scoring. Rule four: the score field must be an integer between 1 and 5. Rule five: the email draft must include the lead's specific question or comment in the first paragraph. Rule six: if any tool returns an error, note the error in the output and continue with available data.
890|
891|Each rule exists because an earlier version of the agent violated it. Rule one exists because the agent once enriched a company that was already in CRM, wasting a tool call and returning redundant data. Rule three exists because the agent once scored a lead before looking up the company, giving a high score to someone with no discernible company. Rule six exists because the agent once failed silently when the enrichment tool timed out, producing an empty profile without flagging the issue.
892|
893|The rules are a record of failures. Every time the agent makes a mistake, I add a rule to prevent it from happening again. The rules section grows over time. It started with two rules. It now has fourteen across all agents. Not every rule applies to every agent.
894|
895|The examples section is the most powerful part of the prompt. I include three to five complete examples of the agent doing its job. Each example shows the input, the thought process, the tool calls, and the final output. The examples are real. They come from actual agent runs that were approved by a human.
896|
897|Here is a condensed example from the lead responder prompt.
898|

913|That example took me five minutes to write. It has saved me hours of debugging. The agent now produces outputs that look exactly like that example ninety-three percent of the time.
914|
915|The template works because it replaces ambiguity with structure. Without the role section, the agent does not know its boundaries. Without the rules section, the agent makes the same mistakes repeatedly. Without the examples, the agent invents its own output format and it changes every time.
916|
917|The difference between a works-once prompt and a works-reliably prompt is the investment in rules and examples. A works-once prompt has a role and a single instruction. It works for the first call and degrades from there. A works-reliably prompt has explicit rules for every known failure mode and concrete examples that anchor the output format.
918|
919|I spend about an hour per week on prompt maintenance. I review the logs from the previous week, identify patterns in agent failures, and update the rules or examples for the affected prompts. This is not prompt engineering. It is editing. I am making the instructions clearer based on where the agent went wrong.
920|
921|The single biggest improvement I made to our prompts was removing ambiguity. I replaced "be thorough" with "call the enrichment tool and the scoring tool for every lead." I replaced "be careful with pricing" with "never include pricing in the first email." I replaced "prioritize high-value leads" with "score each lead 1-5 based on company size and message intent."
922|
923|Clear instructions produce reliable agents. Vague instructions produce unreliable agents that occasionally get lucky. The second generation of our prompts was half the length of the first and twice as effective. Brevity forces precision.

925|## Chapter 18 — Testing Without Breaking
926|
927|![Chapter 18 — Testing Without Breaking](images/ch18_testing_agents.png)
928|
929|Here's an anonymized cautionary tale. An agent was deployed to production and immediately sent a hundred emails to the wrong people. Not test emails. Real emails. To real people. With wrong information.
930|
931|It was a reporting agent. It was supposed to send weekly summaries to department heads. It had been tested in a sandbox. It worked perfectly. It was promoted to production. The first batch went to the wrong email list. The agent read the distribution list from the CRM, but it read the internal field name instead of the email field. Every department head got someone else's report.
932|
933|The mistake was not testing with production data. The test used mock data where the email field and the name field happened to have the same values. The agent looked correct in the sandbox and wrong in reality.
934|
935|That incident led to a system called three-stage testing. I have used it for every agent since. No failures in production for over six months.
936|
937|Stage one is safe testing. The agent runs in a fully isolated environment. It has no access to real tools, real data, or real APIs. Every tool call returns mock data. You can test as aggressively as you want without consequences.
938|
939|A safe testing environment uses a separate database with synthetic records. Fake customers, fake emails, fake orders. The agent processes these and produces outputs. I check whether the outputs are structurally correct. Does the lead responder produce the right JSON format? Does the logistics coordinator call the right tools in the right order? Does the contract reviewer flag the right clauses?
940|
941|Safe testing catches format errors, tool call errors, and prompt parsing errors. It does not catch logic errors because the mock data is too clean. Real data is messy. Mock data is tidy. A prompt that works perfectly on tidy mock data can collapse on the first real input with a missing field.
942|
943|Stage two is correct testing. The agent runs in a staging environment that mirrors production. It has access to real tools but operates on a copy of the data. The staging database is a snapshot from the previous week. The email API is set to a test mode that captures all outbound messages without delivering them. The CRM is a sandbox instance with copied records.
944|
945|Correct testing answers two questions. Does the agent make the right decision given real data? Does the agent produce the right output for a human to review?
946|
947|I run stage two for at least fifty agent runs before moving to stage three. Fifty runs is enough to hit the common edge cases. Missing fields. Duplicate records. Unusual formatting. Special characters. Every time the agent fails in stage two, I fix the prompt or add a rule before restarting the count.
948|
949|During correct testing of a lead responder, the agent received a lead with a company name that included a trademark symbol. The enrichment tool could not find the company because the symbol was in the query. The agent returned a partial profile and scored the lead based on incomplete data. We added a rule to strip special characters from company names before calling the enrichment tool. Problem solved in stage two, never seen in production.
950|
951|Stage three is useful testing. The agent runs in production but with a human watchdog. Every output is reviewed before any action is taken. No automated sends. No automated updates. The agent works, but a human gates every output.
952|
953|Stage three lasts one week. Seven days of production data, real conditions, human oversight. I look for two things. First, does the agent produce useful output that passes human review at least ninety percent of the time? Second, does the agent handle the unexpected inputs that did not appear in stage two?
954|
955|The first week of useful testing for the lead responder revealed a problem we had missed. The agent handled English leads well. Spanish leads produced lower quality outputs. The score was often wrong because the agent could not assess the intent from the translated message. We added a language detection step. If the lead message is not in English, the agent flags it for manual handling and skips scoring. That rule went in during the useful testing week.
956|
957|The staging pattern is the infrastructure that enables this testing. We have three environments. Dev is for safe testing. Staging is for correct testing. Prod is for useful testing. Each environment is identical in code and different in data access and tool permissions.
958|
959|Dev uses mock APIs. All tool calls return fake data. The agent can call any tool without consequences.
960|
961|Staging uses real APIs with sandbox credentials. The CRM sandbox. The email test mode. The calendar test tenant. The data is real but the effects are contained.
962|
963|Prod uses real APIs with production credentials but with human approval gates. The agent can suggest anything, but nothing executes without a human saying yes.
964|
965|Promoting an agent from one stage to the next requires passing a checklist. The checklist is specific and short.
966|
967|For stage one to stage two: the agent completes twenty safe test runs with no structural errors. All tool calls are valid. All outputs match the expected format. No crashes.
968|
969|For stage two to stage three: the agent completes fifty staging runs with at least ninety percent correct decisions. Correct means a human reviewer would approve the output without modification. The remaining ten percent are logged and categorized.
970|
971|For stage three to production: the agent completes one week of useful testing with at least ninety percent human approval rate. No incidents involving data loss, wrong recipient, or incorrect pricing output.
972|
973|The checklist lives in a shared document. Every agent has a row. Every promotion has a date and a reviewer name. Nothing moves without a sign-off.
974|
975|The pre-live checklist is the last gate before an agent becomes fully autonomous. It has five items.
976|
977|One: all rules from the testing phase are documented in the prompt. Two: all tools have correct permission tiers. Three: a human reviewer is assigned for the first month. Four: rollback plan exists. If the agent fails, we can disable it and restore the previous workflow within fifteen minutes. Five: monitoring is configured. Metrics are being collected. Alerts are set.
978|
979|I do not skip items on this checklist. I have a scar from the time I skipped item four. The reporting agent went to production, sent wrong emails, I had no rollback plan, and it took four hours to undo the damage. The rollback plan is now item four and it is non-negotiable.
